headline: Van Hollen, once an insider, has started Democrats’ first big fight
author: Liz Goodwin, Erin Cox

paragraphs.text: Two decades ago, Chris Van Hollen was negotiating in back rooms for Democratic spending priorities and rising through the ranks of the House as a loyal lieutenant to Nancy Pelosi, who saw him as a potential successor.

This week, the two-term senator was waging a public challenge to a bid by Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-New York) to become Senate majority leader, harnessing grassroots anger and making himself the focal point of Democrats’ first big internal brawl, only weeks after historic midterm election gains.

The turn from insider to outsider did not happen overnight or in a linear fashion. Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, has long shown an ambitious streak, and he has been building a reputation, especially in recent years, as a progressive and increasingly antiestablishment figure.

But his underdog challenge to Schumer, 75, has raised his stature on the left and drawn suspicions from detractors that he is using the fight to generate enthusiasm for a potential presidential run, which he denies.

“That’s nonsense,” Van Hollen said. “I am not pursuing a bid in 2028.” He noted that the website he created for his leadership bid solicits donations for Democrats who will run to flip Senate seats in 2028.
Van Hollen, 67, said his motives are more transparent and sweeping. He wants a Democratic Party that acts more boldly.

“One of the things that was very clear in this election is that all of our candidates were running on economic populism,” Van Hollen said in an interview in which he labeled Schumer as the “establishment candidate” in the race. “It wasn’t left or right. It was an understanding that we have an economy that is rigged in favor of very wealthy people and special interests against working people, fueled by political corruption.”
The question for Democrats’ next leader, he says, is: “What are you prepared to do?”

For Van Hollen, the answer is taking on the “army of lobbyists in Washington” who he fears will “eat away” at the promises Democratic candidates made to take on health insurance companies and other corporate interests. He wants to hold a debate among Democratic senators on changing the filibuster rule so they could pass more legislation with a simple majority, which could allow Democrats to pass a campaign finance overhaul and raise the minimum wage without needing Republican votes.
Little of it, in all likelihood, would get Trump’s signature. But it would force a policy confrontation many progressives are craving.

Van Hollen’s longshot bid has highlighted Schumer’s weaknesses as many Democrats wonder whether he will face a challenge for his seat from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) in 2028 — or retire.

But even a weakened Schumer likely has the upper hand against Van Hollen’s insurgent message. The expanded Democratic caucus includes new lawmakers from red states who distanced themselves from Schumer on the trail, but who may also be wary of backing someone who is running to Schumer’s left.

Van Hollen has said he thinks he has at least 15 of the 28 Democratic senator votes he’d need to become leader, and has acknowledged Schumer has the advantage in the race. Only five senators have publicly backed Van Hollen so far, but grassroots activists are calling and urging more to join them.
“We have a lot of momentum,” Van Hollen said.
From insider to renegade

Van Hollen, whose upbringing included stints across the globe as the son of a diplomat, was first elected to public office more than three decades ago, emerging from a crowded primary to win a Maryland House of Delegates seat before taking on his mentor to ascend to the state senate.

In 2002 he was elected to the House by toppling the establishment pick from the Kennedy political dynasty, Mark K. Shriver, in the primary. Van Hollen amassed power quickly there, serving as a lead budget negotiator during the Obama administration and twice chairing the House Democrats’ campaign arm.
“There were many people in the Congress who thought he might be the next speaker after me,” Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-California), said in an interview last year.

His Maryland colleague, Donna F. Edwards, then a congresswoman, was part of Van Hollen’s operation to secure support to become the next speaker. But he jettisoned that path in order to run against her for an open Senate seat in 2016. He beat Edwards, who was seen as to the left of Van Hollen on Israel at the time, in a primary she described in an interview as “noxious and toxic.”

“This guy, he’s had a challenging election every time he’s moved up,” said former Maryland Attorney General Brian E. Frosh, whose career overlapped with Van Hollen’s. “It’s easy to underestimate him. He’s a giant killer.”

In the Senate, Van Hollen was mostly a loyal Democratic foot soldier, helping chair the party’s campaign arm in 2018 and steering millions home to Maryland as a member of the appropriations committee.

But in late 2023, Van Hollen began breaking with his party on Israel, increasingly questioning President Joe Biden’s unconditional support as the war with Hamas devolved into a humanitarian crisis in Gaza.
In early 2025, when Democrats were reeling from Trump’s win, Van Hollen began criticizing Schumer, and taking bold stands on immigration and Israel that clashed with party orthodoxy.

In April that year, he traveled to a notorious El Salvador prison to visit Kilmar Abrego García, a Maryland resident the Trump administration deported to El Salvador despite an order barring his removal there. (Van Hollen was turned away from the prison, but allowed to meet with him at a nearby hotel.) At the time, some Democrats were warning the party should downplay immigration issues and focus on the economy.
“That was about taking a courageous stance in the face of the conventional wisdom that now seems very outmoded,” said Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minnesota), who is retiring.

In September that year, Van Hollen obliquely criticized Schumer and Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries for failing to endorse Zohran Mamdani in New York, after he had won his primary. “That kind of spineless politics is what people are sick of,” Van Hollen told a crowd of cheering activists in Des Moines.
His stances earned him new progressive fans and changed his reputation from insider to rabble rouser.

“For a long time he was seen as a kind of consummate inside legislator,” said Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Maryland), the incoming chair of the House Judiciary Committee. “And now he is seen as somebody fully in the progressive resistance to Trump and a leader on a whole bunch of different things, including immigration and human rights.”

But the substance of that pivot has alienated some longtime supporters. Former state senator Bobby Zirkin, a moderate Democrat, has criticized Van Hollen sharply over Israel since the senator began calling for conditioning military aid to the nation. After Van Hollen announced his leadership plans, Zirkin wrote an op-ed in the Baltimore Sun saying the senator pursued “power over morality.”
“He goes where he thinks the wind is going,” Zirkin said in an interview.
But Edwards, who battled Van Hollen for his Senate seat and mended fences with him, said in an interview that she encouraged him to challenge Schumer over the summer.
“Chris represents the boldness that voters spoke to for this election,” Edwards said.
An outside campaign ruffles insider feathers
Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Michigan) has also been urging on Van Hollen’s challenge this year, and on Tuesday made the case again to about 100 online influencers.

“The most important conversation isn’t just a conversation between 56 senators; it’s a conversation between the 56 senators and the hundreds of millions of people who elected us all,” El-Sayed said in an interview.

Van Hollen and his supporters have sought to channel the activist anger with party leadership through groups such as MoveOn and Indivisible, whose leaders have endorsed Van Hollen and whose members are calling their senators to demand they back him, too.

“If you were to have a vote today with the Democratic base and say, choose between Senator Schumer and Senator Van Hollen, I would say that Van Hollen would probably win in a landslide,” said Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), who is backing Van Hollen.
The tactic has annoyed some lawmakers. It may also have its limits, given the insular nature of the election.

Van Hollen’s Democratic colleague from Maryland, Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, announced this week that she is supporting Schumer, saying he had asked for her support before Van Hollen entered the race. As online anger with Alsobrooks boiled, Van Hollen released a statement Thursday saying he did not want the discussion around her vote to involve “vitriol or hostility.”

Van Hollen has vowed to mostly stay out of Democratic primaries if elected leader, noting that El-Sayed and Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan from Minnesota would not be elected if Schumer’s preferred primary candidates had won. Both progressive freshmen are backing Van Hollen. Other newly elected Democrats from more conservative areas worry the dispute could tarnish their efforts to push back on the war, inflation, and other issues that fueled their victories.
Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D-South Carolina) compared the leadership clash to two surgeons arguing about a procedure while a patient was bleeding in the trauma bay.
“Really what we need is someone just to stop the bleeding,” she told reporters.
Andrews has not said whom she is supporting.
Theodoric Meyer contributed to this report.
